title: Asking for someone absent
hook: an angel says, and for you the same, when you pray for someone behind their back (Muslim)

segments.voice: Yesterday: hasanah, the short du'a from Surah al-Baqarah. Good here, good there: not one or the other, both.

Being talked about behind your back usually means gossip. A comment in a group chat you weren't supposed to see. A silence when you walk into the room. Now turn it around. Someone you barely think about has been saying your name, quietly, for a long time, asking for good things for you. You never knew. They never told you. There's a hadith about exactly that, and it adds a twist: someone else is listening. Today: ameen.
screen: `TALKED ABOUT BEHIND YOUR BACK.` → `NOW TURN IT AROUND.` → `SOMEONE ELSE IS LISTENING.`

segments.voice: Sahih Muslim reports it from Abu al-Darda', one of the companions. The Prophet ﷺ said: whenever a Muslim makes du'a for his brother in his absence, behind his back, an angel says: ameen, and for you the same. In Arabic, wa laka bi-mithl: and for you, its like. The moment you ask for good for someone who can't hear you, the same good is asked for you. Not by you. By an angel. Another version in Muslim adds that an angel is appointed at the person's head for just this purpose. Why does the absence matter? Because there's no credit in it. The other person will never thank you, and you can't be doing it to look kind. A report in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi, which some scholars grade weak, goes further: the du'a answered most quickly is the one made by someone absent for someone absent. The Qur'an itself is full of people asking for others. Ibrahim asks forgiveness for himself, his parents and the believers. Surah al-Hashr describes later believers asking forgiveness for those who came before them in faith, people they never met. And notice how the hadith is phrased. It isn't a deal offered in advance. It describes what happens: someone goes out of their way for another person, and finds they've been included.
screen: `AN ANGEL SAYS: AND FOR YOU THE SAME.` · `NO CREDIT, NO THANKS.` · `IBRAHIM ASKS FOR HIS PARENTS.` · `YOU FIND YOU'VE BEEN INCLUDED.` · then, large: `WA LAKA BI-MITHL.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who has no idea you're thinking of them: a coworker who seems tired, a neighbor you only wave at, someone you've fallen out with. If you pray, ask Allah for one good thing for them, silently, in your own words; if you don't, simply wish them one good thing, as specifically as you can. Don't tell them afterward; let it stay behind their back.
Ameen, so be it: what the hadith says an angel answers whenever you make du'a for someone absent, behind their back, and for you the same.
Your line: and the same for you. Behind their back, an angel is listening. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Muslims make du'a for family, friends and fellow believers by name in their private prayers, without telling them, following the hadith that an angel says 'and for you the same'.

fork.reveal: the angel's answer is wa laka bi-mithl, and for you its like (Muslim 2732). the one who asks finds they've been included.

original.note: Arabic: and for you, its like, the angel's words in the hadith.

trapdoor: what you thought: praying for others is a nice extra.
what it means: a du'a made in someone's absence has no credit in it, and an angel asks the same for you.
what a scholar hears: bi-zahr al-ghayb, 'behind the back of the absent' (Muslim 2732–2733); and 14:41 and 59:10 in the Qur'an.
recall: a festival, from a root for returning
